newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada adds terrorism charge to a detained Saudi.
newsitem.headline: Canada adds terrorism charge to a detained Saudi.

text.p: The Canadian government on Wednesday charged a Saudi citizen, Fahad al-Shehri, whom it has detained since December, with being a terrorist.
The new charge was laid in a hearing on whether to grant refugee status to Shehri, one of two Saudi dissidents being held in Ottawa.

The other Saudi being detained in the same Ottawa prison is Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, whom the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation has named in connection with a bombing in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. airmen in June.
Dianne Toikko, presenting the case against Shehri for the government, said there were reasonable grounds "to believe that he is a person who has engaged in terrorism."
He had already been held on the grounds that he had belonged to a group that engaged in terrorism, but this new charge would pin responsibility on him directly if it stuck.
She did not immediately elaborate on the charge but it may stem from whether he bought weapons for Moslem fighters.

Shehri arrived at the Ottawa airport on Dec. 6, and according to the government's understanding of his initial remarks he claimed that Saudi Arabia wanted him in connection with the June bombing, in which he denied any involvement.

Immigration officials also understood him to say he was part of a mujahideen (holy warriors) group and that he collected money and guns for this group, Citizenship and Immigration spokeswoman Joanne John said.

Shehri, who was born in 1976, told Toikko that he did relief work in Afghanistan with the opposition Tajik group Renaissance Party, which he said was using force to combat the Moscow-backed Tajik government.

"I don't think that is considered violence. It's considered defending one's rights," said Shehri, sitting in a dark-blue prison uniform and light-blue sneakers across the table from Toikko in the prison chapel.
But he gave no evidence on Wednesday morning of personally engaging in any armed activity or of buying weapons. The hearing was likely to last into next week.

He said through an interpreter that he was sent to Afghanistan from Riyadh along with a Saudi government official and other Saudis by the World Youth Congress, which he described as a reputable organisation that engaged in relief work around the world.

Shehri -- clean-cut, with a neat goatee, moustache and gold-rimmed glasses -- said he bought things like food, tents and generators for Tajik orphans and refugees who fled to Afghanistan from the former Soviet republic.
Shehri's lawyer, Douglas Baum, told reporters that he believed the whole incident was due to a misunderstanding.

He said Shehri indeed opposed the Saudi government and had worked with various Moslem groups in Afghanistan, Azerbaijan and Bosnia, but was sent over as an accredited representative of relief organisations. Shehri also had contact in England with Saudi dissident groups, Baum said.

"I think that what we've had here is a failure to communicate," Baum said, noting that Shehri's initial statement was translated by an off-duty police officer at the airport rather than an accredited translator.
"I don't think the translation was reliable. There seems to be some dispute about what was said."
Baum said Shehri, a member of the majority Sunni division of Islam, had no connection with Sayegh, a follower of the Shi'ite sect dominant in Iran.
The lawyer said the United States had shown only passing interest in Shehri and the Saudis had shown no interest.
